text: You have one free hour at the IP Week 2026 Marketplace. Where do you go first?

options.label: The booth using quantum fluid dynamics to predict which line at the supermarket cashier will move the fastest.
The booth with a brand name so deliciously sticky that you remember it after forgetting everything else.
The flashy installation that was designed for social media.
The booth with exquisitely designed products.

text: Your team has invented a hawker-table booking system. What do you do next?

options.label: Before the yacht-purchasing, do some proper research to make sure no one else has got there first.
The world is not ready for this. We keep it exclusively for use in our staff canteen.
Brainstorm a catchy name for it before somebody defaults to 'Project Final FINAL_2'.
We open-source it for the benefit of humanity – after issuing a press release to ensure humanity knows who to thank.

text: Your primary competitor launches something that looks uncomfortably familiar to your product. What bothers you most?

options.label: They stole the idea for our top-secret thingamajig!
Customers are getting confused (as customers do).
The blurb on the back of their product box is a copy of ours, including the typo that states '[insert compelling customer testimonial]'.
Their invention isn't even new! My nephew made that his art and crafts class!

text: A venture capitalist asks what makes your enterprise commercially unique. What do you lead with?

options.label: Our technical processes.
Years of accumulated goodwill and the courageous decision to never burden our marketing campaigns with anything related to the actual product.
Your overworked team producing training manuals and proprietary software algorithms.
The product looks so refined that customers will pay twice as much for functionality they already own.

text: Your company develops a premium new coffee plant variety. What is the commercial plan?

options.label: A marketing campaign around the misty hillside where the plant originates.
Consistency is the key. Our coffee plant has been successfully bred in the International Space Station, the bottom of the Marianas Trench, and a McDonald's bathroom.
Creativity! A multi-movie cinematic franchise starring your coffee bean.
We share the love by freely distributing seeds of our highly-invasive variety to our competitors.

text: Your product is great, but sales are still low. What do you think needs fixing?

options.label: Customers cannot remember its name. Neither can the writer of this personality quiz. Or you, for that matter.
Your product's origin story begins and ends with 'manufactured somewhere with favourable overheads'.
Your lifestyle product isn't Instagrammable enough.
You spent too much on commissioning an original orchestral symphony that plays whenever the app opens. This has left very little money to address how frequently it crashes.

text: You have been in product development for five years and still aren't ready to go to market. What keeps you going?

options.label: Consistent growth. Your products finally work without the engineering team whispering words of encouragement.
Competition. We finally proved our invention doesn't infringe a competitor's.
Total operational security. The proprietary process is documented nowhere and understood by no one.
Charity. You forge on in the knowledge that your work will become the foundation for the next generation.

text: Your team is presenting the product at Singapore IP Week. What keeps you awake the night before?

options.label: Your lead engineer insists on presenting an AI-generated 'conceptual diagram' but nobody can agree on who owns the rights to the image, if any.
The prototype looks great from the front, but the booth permits visitors to walk around it.
The audience may clap during the presentation but forget your company's name after leaving.
Your junior inserted confidential technical information into Slide 14 but the custom slide transitions are too elaborate to safely remove them.

text: Your business is ready to expand overseas. What is the first strategic question you think should be addressed?

options.label: How many foreign markets can we afford to dive into?
Will consumers still pay a premium if our heritage product is no longer crafted in a tiny Italian valley?
Will our business take root in foreign soil or will it wither and die on the vine?
If we make the underlying design free, can we trick the entire industry into adopting it as the global standard?
